Q: Floyds Triangle with a sorted array (Python) A:

The last number of any row of Floyd's Triangle is the integer sum of the row number. r*(r+1)//2 The starting number of that row is 1 + (stop - r) For range just add one to stop and get range(stop-r,stop). Recursively count down rows by one until we get to 1.

   
def FloydsList(r): 
    if r <= 1: return [[1]] 
    stop = r * (r+1) // 2 + 1
    return FloydsList(r-1) + [[j for j in range(stop-r,stop)]]

# Print Floyd's Triangles until Enter    
while True:
    print("Print a Floyd's Triangle <Enter> to quit") 
    try: rows = int(input("Number of Rows?> ")) 
    except: break
    print(FloydsList(rows) )

Output:

Q: How can I join two Git histories together A:

It's doable with varying levels of difficulty.

  • If you care about preserving the committer name, email, and timestamp, then you'll need to do more intensive scripting. This is because git-rebase replaces those fields with your user and current timestamp, while retaining the author name, email, and timestamp. You might want to get familiar with the environment variables GIT_COMMITTER_NAME, GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL, GIT_COMMITTER_DATE.

    I've done similar rewriting of Git repositories in the past, and I wrote a low-level Git object manipulation library in Java to get precisely the semantics I want - which is a ton of effort that I don't wish upon anybody.

  • Else if the state of files in D1 differs from C100, then I haven't fleshed out or tested this case. There will probably be a lot of overlap with the next case.

  • Else (the state of all files in C100 exactly matches the state of D1 so it's a true copy), then follow these instructions:

    1. Take note of the hashes of commits C100 and D50, as we will use them soon.
    2. All manipulation will be done in RepoC.
    3. git fetch /path/to/RepoD to grab all the new commits and underlying objects.
    4. git reset --hard D50 to move the current branch to the new tip of development.
    5. git rebase C100 to take all the changes and commits strictly after D1 and up to and including D50 (i.e. --D2--D3-...-D50) and append it to C100 (i.e. ...-C100--D2--D3-...-D50). For each new commit, all author information is retained, but all committer information is replaced by you and the current timestamp. You can see that with git log --format=fuller.

Q: Java Web Application "Event Listener for Expired Sessions" A:

javax.servlet.http.HttpSessionListener

The Jakarta Servlet specification provides a listener interface for session expiring: HttpSessionListener.

You write a class that implements the two methods on that interface. Mark your class with the annotation @WebListener to have your class automatically instantiated by your servlet container. When a session expires, the servlet container automatically invokes the sessionDestroyed method on the instance of your class.

There in that sessionDestroyed method, you can take any actions you want such as writing to your database.

@WebListener
public class AwesomeAppSessionListener implements HttpSessionListener 
{
    /**
     * Called when a session is ending.
     * 
     * @param se the HttpSessionEvent containing the session
     */
    @Override
    public void sessionDestroyed( HttpSessionEvent sessionEvent ) 
    {
        String sessionId = sessionEvent.getSession().getId();
        String timestamp = Instant.now().toString();
        
        IO.println( "Session Destroyed - ID: " + sessionId + " at " + timestamp );
    }
}

The Jakarta Servlet spec provides several such listener interfaces. You can see them listed on that @WebListener annotation’s Javadoc.

Context (your web app):

  • ServletContextListener
  • ServletContextAttributeListener

Request:

  • ServletRequestListener
  • ServletRequestAttributeListener

Session:

  • HttpSessionListener
  • HttpSessionAttributeListener
  • HttpSessionIdListener

In particular, ServletContextListener gives you hooks for when your web app (a “context” in servlet-speak) is launching (contextInitialized), and when your web app is shutting down (contextDestroyed). So you can perform app-wide setup and teardown operations. Those operations would go in the two methods you write in a class implementing that interface.
